desc:
Cities are labelled 1 to n. Two different cities a and b are joined by a road exactly when they have a common divisor strictly greater than threshold, i.e. gcd(a, b) > threshold.

For each query [a, b] decide whether one can travel from city a to city b along these roads, possibly through other cities. Return an array with 1 for reachable and 0 for not reachable, one entry per query.

n = 6, threshold = 2
queries = [[4,5],[3,6],[2,4]]

result = [0,1,0]

With threshold 2, the only road is 3-6 (gcd 3). With threshold 0 every pair of cities would have a road, since every gcd is at least 1.
constraints: queries[j] = [a, b] with 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
hints: Building the road list by testing every pair with gcd costs O(n² log n) which is too slow for n = 20,000. Find a way to generate only the useful roads.
Two cities share a divisor z > threshold exactly when both are multiples of such a z. So all multiples of one z belong to the same group.
For every z from threshold + 1 to n, union z with 2z, 3z, ... using union-find. Then each query is find(a) == find(b). This is a sieve-like loop with about n log n unions.
editorial: Instead of testing all pairs, flip the question around: for a fixed z > threshold, every pair of multiples of z has gcd at least z and so is connected. It is enough to connect z with each of its multiples 2z, 3z, ..., because all multiples are then in one set through z. Doing this for every z from threshold + 1 to n adds all roads' worth of connectivity.

A pair with gcd(a, b) = g > threshold is covered by z = g, since both are multiples of g; conversely every union we perform corresponds to a real road. The loops perform about n · (1/1 + 1/2 + ...) = O(n log n) unions in the worst case (threshold 0), each nearly constant time. Queries are then answered by comparing roots.
